lesson.title: Arsenal of Democracy: The Lend-Lease Act
lesson.summary: Signed in March 1941, the Lend-Lease Act let the United States supply Britain and other Allied nations with weapons and equipment without requiring immediate payment, moving the officially neutral United States much closer to the Allied side.
lesson.body:
Even after the Neutrality Act of 1939 allowed cash and carry arms sales, Britain's gold and dollar reserves were running low by late 1940 after more than a year of war against Germany, and cash and carry alone could not sustain the level of support Britain needed to keep fighting after France's surrender.

In a fireside chat radio address in December 1940, Roosevelt argued that the United States should become the arsenal of democracy, supplying weapons and equipment so Britain could keep fighting without American troops joining the war directly. He compared the arrangement to lending a garden hose to a neighbor whose house was on fire, an analogy meant to present the aid as practical neighborliness rather than a step toward war.

Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act into law on March 11, 1941. It authorized the president to lend, lease, or transfer war materiel to any country whose defense he judged vital to American security, without requiring payment up front. The program later expanded well beyond Britain, extending to the Soviet Union after Germany invaded it in June 1941, and eventually to China and other Allied nations.

Lend-Lease marked a clear break from strict neutrality, tying American industrial production directly to the Allied war effort even before Pearl Harbor pulled the United States into direct combat. It built on an earlier arrangement from September 1940, in which the United States had traded a group of aging destroyers to Britain in exchange for access to British military bases.
